beginner: The most common microgreen problem. In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants right at the base, and you often see fuzzy white or gray mold on the surface. Arugula's crowded leaves and sticky-when-wet seed make good airflow and careful watering matter even more.

beginner: The arugula you will almost always grow as a microgreen is regular salad arugula (Eruca sativa). It is one of the fastest microgreens, ready in about 6 to 8 days, with a bold peppery flavor. Its seeds get sticky and gel-like when wet, so mist them instead of soaking, or they clump. There is also a wild or wasabi arugula (Diplotaxis) that grows more slowly and tastes even spicier. Whichever you pick, use seed sold for sprouting or microgreens, and cut while the little seed-leaves are open for the best flavor.
seasoned: Almost all arugula sold as a microgreen is standard salad arugula (Eruca sativa): a fast brassica, roughly 6 to 8 days to a peppery cut, sown at about 10 g per 1020 tray with no presoak. The seed is mucilaginous and forms a gel coat when wet, so mist it rather than soaking it, or it clumps and germinates unevenly. Wild or wasabi arugula (Diplotaxis tenuifolia) is a different genus that runs slower and tastes sharper; treat it the same way at sowing but expect a longer, spicier crop. Use untreated, microgreen-grade or food-safe seed, and cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, before true leaves and fiber turn the flavor harsh.

Arugula is one of the fastest microgreens, typically 6 to 8 days in a warm, brightly lit setup and up to about 10 to 12 days in cooler or lower-light home conditions. beginner: To always have arugula microgreens ready, start a new tray every few days instead of one big batch. Because they grow indoors and finish so fast, you can keep this going all year.
seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh tray every 3 to 5 days rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space, and arugula's short 6 to 8 day cycle turns trays over quickly.

beginner: Arugula microgreens are baby arugula plants that you harvest very young, when they are just a couple of inches tall, for a bold peppery, spicy flavor. They are one of the fastest microgreens to grow: scatter about 10 grams of seed thickly on a damp tray, cover it to keep it dark for a day or two while the seeds sprout, then move it into bright light to green up, and snip in about 6 to 8 days (a bit longer in a cool or dim room). Arugula seed gets sticky when wet, so mist it instead of soaking. You grow them indoors all year on a shallow tray of seed-starting mix or a special growing mat, so there is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, and they grow the same way no matter where you live. Use them fresh on salads, sandwiches, and as a garnish.
seasoned: Arugula microgreens are the young seedlings of arugula (Eruca sativa, in the mustard family), harvested at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage for a concentrated, distinctly peppery, spicy bite that is the whole reason to grow them. They are among the fastest microgreens: a dense, even sow of about 10 g per 1020 tray, a short blackout of about 1 to 2 days to even the stand, then 18 hours of light to green up, cut in roughly 6 to 8 days (longer, closer to 10 to 12 days, in cooler or lower-light rooms). The seed is small and mucilaginous, so it is misted rather than presoaked, or it clumps. Grown indoors year-round on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat, arugula microgreens need no frost, season, or hardiness zone, so the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere. They are used fresh as a peppery salad base, sandwich layer, or garnish.

beginner: Your arugula microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and, for many, the first true leaf is just showing, usually about 6 to 8 days after sowing and around 1 to 2 inches tall. Cut them while they are young for the best peppery flavor, before the bigger leaves come in. Snip them just above the soil with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so you start a new tray each time.
seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically about 6 to 8 days from sowing (up to roughly 10 to 12 in cooler or lower light), when the stand is a couple of inches tall and bright green. Harvest before the true leaves and stem fiber develop, since that is when the flavor shifts from pleasantly peppery to harsh. Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
